walkthroughs.body_html:
Aquinas (1225-1274) opens the Summa Theologica with the question whether God exists. His five ways are: from motion, from efficient causation, from contingency, from gradation of being, and from governance of things.

Each is a posteriori, beginning with observation and concluding with God as first principle.

In Proslogion 2 (1078), Anselm defines God as 'that than which nothing greater can be conceived' and argues that this being must exist in reality, not merely in the mind.

In Proslogion 3, he sharpens the argument: God's existence is necessary; He cannot even be conceived not to exist.

In Natural Theology (1802), Paley argues that finding a watch on a heath forces an inference to a watchmaker.

The 'contrivances' of nature (the eye, the heart, even astronomy) reveal an even greater designer, the God of classical theism.

mcqs.q: What distinction matters for the free will defence to the problem of evil?
options: Between moral evil (caused by free human choices) and natural evil (earthquakes, disease) — the free will defence directly addresses moral evil but struggles with natural evil, which isn't a product of free choice.
Aquinas's Five Ways are five Christian sacraments.
The free will defence solves all forms of evil at once.
Natural evil means evil that is good for nature.

mcqs.q: What is the problem of evil?
options: Natural evil means evil that is good for nature.
It is the question of whether evil people will go to hell.
It is the question of whether the devil really exists.
If God is all-loving, all-knowing and all-powerful, why does evil and suffering exist? Logically, all four cannot be true together without explanation.

The Kalam cosmological argument differs from Aquinas's Third Way because it:
options: depends on the claim that the universe began to exist at some point in time
argues from the contingency of beings without any claim about a beginning
is an a priori argument from the definition of God
concludes that the universe needs no explanation

mcqs.q: Gaunilo's 'perfect island' objection is intended to show that:
options: Anselm's reasoning would absurdly prove the existence of any perfect thing one defines
islands are more perfect than God
the ontological argument is empirically verifiable
necessary existence belongs only to islands

mcqs.q: Hume's principle that 'like effects prove like causes' implies the design argument supports, at most:
options: a finite, possibly imperfect designer or team of designers — not the infinite God of classical theism
the omnipotent and omniscient God of the Bible
the non-existence of any designer
a designer who must also be the first cause
